title: Virology in Low-Resource Settings
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Clinically focused virology for East African wards: recognise common viral infections, use limited diagnostics, and apply first‑line treatments while avoiding drug interactions and toxicity.

sections.p: Virology is the study of viruses, small infectious agents that replicate inside host cells. In low‑resource hospitals, the most common viral illnesses are malaria‑like fevers, hepatitis B, HIV, and emerging arboviruses.
b: Viruses are acellular, need host machinery
Diagnosis often limited to serology or rapid tests

sections.p: Viruses are nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat; some have envelopes. Their replication cycles are short and highly efficient.
b: Enveloped viruses are more fragile outside host

t.b: Positive indicates current infection; negative does not rule out if low viral load
Positive = likely infection; false negatives common in low viral load

sections.p: Viruses spread by direct contact, droplets, vectors, or blood. Once inside a cell, they hijack the host machinery to produce progeny.
b: Entry via specific receptors (e.g., CD4 for HIV)
Assembly and release by budding or lysis

t.b: Positive = chronic carrier or active disease

sections.p: Common viral diseases in East Africa include hepatitis B, HIV, dengue, chikungunya, and emerging coronaviruses. Symptoms overlap with bacterial infections, complicating diagnosis.
Clinical suspicion is key; confirm with affordable tests. When tests are unavailable, use epidemiology and symptom clusters.

t.b: Positive = acute dengue; negative does not exclude late infection
Positive = confirm with ELISA or PCR if possible

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and prevent transmission. Drug choice balances efficacy, toxicity, and availability.

t.b: Reduces viral load; monitor renal function
Avoid in pregnancy; monitor for CNS effects

sections.p: Remember that many viral infections mimic bacterial sepsis. Use simple bedside tests and epidemiology to guide management when labs are limited.
b: For dengue, monitor platelet trend; a drop <50,000 warrants transfusion

whenToSeekHelp: Severe jaundice with vomiting and confusion
Severe respiratory distress in a patient with known viral infection

faq.q: How do I differentiate dengue from malaria clinically?
faq.a: Dengue has severe headache, retro‑orbital pain, rash, and thrombocytopenia; malaria has fever spikes, chills, and hemoglobin drop.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing suspected HIV in a resource‑poor setting?
faq.a: Perform a rapid antibody test; if positive, start ART immediately while awaiting confirmatory tests.

faq.q: Can I use NSAIDs in dengue?
faq.a: No; NSAIDs increase bleeding risk. Use paracetamol for fever and pain.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with fever, headache, and a maculopapular rash after returning from a rural area. What is the most likely diagnosis and first test? — Dengue; test: NS1 antigen RDT.
A patient with chronic hepatitis B is on tenofovir. She develops worsening renal function. What should you do? — Discontinue tenofovir; switch to entecavir.
A child has fever, vomiting, and abdominal pain. You suspect viral hepatitis. What bedside sign helps differentiate it from bacterial gastroenteritis? — Jaundice.
A 35‑year‑old man with HIV presents with fever and weight loss. What opportunistic infection should you rule out first? — Tuberculosis.
You have a patient with suspected chikungunya. What supportive care is essential? — Aggressive fluid management and analgesia with paracetamol.
A patient with suspected viral meningitis has a normal CSF opening pressure. What does this suggest? — Early disease; still treat supportively and monitor.
